newsitem.title: GERMANY: German '96 insolvencies climb again to record high.
newsitem.headline: German '96 insolvencies climb again to record high.

text.p: In the latest sign of Germany's sluggish economy, the Federal Statistics Office reported on Wednesday that the number of insolvencies in 1996 had reached a record high for the fourth straight year.
The office said that led by bankruptcies among building firms as well as hotels and restaurants, the total number of insolvencies climbed 9.3 percent during 1996 to 31,471.
East Germany, where the country's economic difficulties are especially pronounced, posted the most dramatic insolvency increases, up 18.7 percent to 8,393. Some 7,419 of those were companies.
In west Germany, where the construction sector plays a less important role in the economy, the number of insolvencies last year climbed 6.3 percent to 23,078, 18,111 of those being companies.
But even amid the gloom, there may be signs that the worst may be over for German companies and households.

Insolvencies in the last part of the year showed the trend moderating. In December insolvencies fell 5.8 percent from a year ago to 2,539 and in November, they had increased only one percent to 2,501.
"The insolvency growth rates (in 1996) of 9.3 percent overall and 14.3 percent for companies are clearly weaker than in the last five years," the office said in a statement.
Economists link the insolvency rate to Germany's record high levels of joblessness. Longer unemployment lines reduce household incomes and final demand.
But the jobless front may offer relief on insolvencies.

Although unemployment rose 5,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.316 million in February, the increase appeared to signal a moderating trend and raised hopes that the worst of Germany's job crisis may be over.

Labour Office Bernhard Jagoda said earlier this month that he expected a decline in unemployment in March and that broader employment conditions are improving, especially among manufacturing companies.
